lessons.title: Ich lasse mein Fahrrad reparieren: lassen = have something done
lessons.goal: Say what you do yourself and what you have done by a service, with all present forms of lassen and the infinitive at the end.

grammar.point: lassen + infinitive means that someone else does the work for you: Ich lasse mein Fahrrad reparieren. lassen stands in position 2, the infinitive at the very end, like with a modal verb, and there is no zu. du lässt and er/sie/es lässt have an umlaut.

mistake.wrong: Ich lasse mein Fahrrad zu reparieren.
mistake.why: lassen works like a modal verb: the plain infinitive goes to the end, with no zu.

terms.meaning: have something done: someone else does the work, you organise it
yourself: you do the work
a small unstressed word that adds surprise or agreement: Das ist ja praktisch!

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich repariere' to 'Ich lasse reparieren'
cards.body: This chapter is called Das ist ja praktisch! (That is really handy!). It is about services, buying and things that break. Leon's bike is broken. He could repair it himself, or he could pay someone to do it. For the second idea German uses one verb: lassen. It works like a modal verb.
steps: You already know: Leon muss sein Fahrrad reparieren. A modal verb stands in position 2, the infinitive goes to the very end.
New today: Leon lässt sein Fahrrad reparieren. lassen stands in position 2, the infinitive at the end, and someone else does the work. There is no zu, unlike Es ist schwer, das Fahrrad zu reparieren.
By the end you can: say what you do yourself and what you have done by a service, with all forms of lassen.

examples.de: Leon muss sein Fahrrad reparieren.
examples.en: Leon has to repair his bike.
examples.why: You know this: modal verb in position 2, infinitive at the end. Leon does the work.

examples.de: Leon lässt sein Fahrrad reparieren.
examples.en: Leon is having his bike repaired.
examples.why: New today: the same frame with lassen. Now a mechanic does the work.

cards.more: Think of the title: Das ist ja praktisch! The little word ja does not mean yes here. It adds surprise or agreement, a bit like 'oh, that is really handy!'. You will hear it from Mira today. The grammar of the day is easy to picture because you already own the frame. Muss, kann and will push an infinitive to the end. lassen does exactly the same. The only new thing is the meaning: you organise the job, another person does it. And remember: lassen never takes zu.

cards.title: Leon's problem: a flat tyre and bad brakes
cards.body: Leon wants to ride to the university, but his bike has a flat tyre and the brakes do not work. He has no tools and no time. So he takes the bike to the bike shop around the corner. Many people in Berlin do this: they pay a service.
cards.lead: First the story of today: Leon, his broken bike and the bike shop. These words come back in every card, so the grammar later has a clear picture.

examples.de: Mein Fahrrad hat einen Platten.
examples.en: My bike has a flat tyre.

examples.de: Die Bremse funktioniert nicht.
examples.en: The brake does not work.

examples.de: Der Fahrradladen ist gleich um die Ecke.
examples.en: The bike shop is just around the corner.

deeper.text: Einen Platten haben is everyday spoken German, short for a flat tyre. The word is masculine, der Platten, and it almost always comes with haben: Ich habe einen Platten. On a bike you say das Fahrrad, but in speech people very often shorten it to das Rad. Both are neuter. Mit dem Rad fahren and Rad fahren (to cycle) are just as common as Fahrrad fahren.

example.de: Ich fahre jeden Tag mit dem Rad zur Uni.
example.en: I ride my bike to uni every day.

cards.more: Picture Leon on a Monday morning. He goes down to the courtyard, takes his bike and sees it: the front tyre is completely flat. He tests the brake and nothing happens. He looks for tools in the WG, but there are none, and his lecture starts in forty minutes. What can he do? He pushes the bike to the little shop around the corner. Keep this scene in your head: one problem, no tools, no time, and a service that helps.
steps: Das Fahrrad hat einen Platten.
Die Bremsen sind kaputt.
Leon hat kein Werkzeug und keine Zeit.
Er bringt das Fahrrad in den Fahrradladen.

cards.title: Do it yourself or have it done: selbst or lassen
cards.body: Two ways to deal with a job. Do it yourself: the normal verb plus selbst. Have it done: lassen plus the infinitive at the end. With lassen you are the boss: you decide, someone else does the work, and usually you pay for it.
cards.lead: Leon has two choices: repair the bike himself or pay the shop. This card puts both sentences side by side, so you see what lassen changes.

examples.de: Ich wasche das Auto selbst.
examples.en: I wash the car myself.

examples.de: Ich lasse das Auto waschen.
examples.en: I have the car washed.

examples.de: Anna lässt ihre Bilder rahmen.
examples.en: Anna has her pictures framed.

deeper.text: selbst can stand at the end or right after the person: Ich repariere das selbst or Ich selbst repariere das (I myself). In speech you also hear selber, which means the same and is very common in the south. One thing selbst never does is change the verb. Only lassen moves the work to another person, so Ich lasse das selbst reparieren sounds strange.

example.de: Das mache ich lieber selber.
example.en: I would rather do that myself.

cards.more: Compare it with English. I repair the bike: I do it. I have the bike repaired, or I get the bike repaired: someone else does it. English needs have or get plus a past participle. German is simpler: lassen plus the plain infinitive at the end, the dictionary form. So you never need a new verb form. Ich lasse das Auto waschen, Anna lässt ihre Bilder rahmen. You keep the same infinitive, you only add lassen in position 2.

cards.title: The forms of lassen: du lässt, er lässt
cards.body: lassen is irregular in two forms only. With du and er/sie/es the a becomes ä: du lässt, er lässt. It is the same change as fahren, du fährst, er fährt. All other forms keep the a: ich lasse, wir lassen, ihr lasst, sie lassen.
cards.lead: Now you know what lassen means. This card shows how it changes with each person, because two forms get an umlaut.

examples.de: Lässt du deine Haare schneiden?
examples.en: Are you having your hair cut?

examples.de: Wir lassen die Pizza liefern.
examples.en: We are having the pizza delivered.

examples.de: Lasst ihr den Computer reparieren?
examples.en: Are you having the computer repaired?

deeper.text: Listen to the vowel: lassen and lasst have a short a, lässt has a short ä, like the e in Bett. The double s stays after a short vowel, so you write lässt and lasst with ss, never with ß. Careful with ihr lasst and du lässt: they look similar, but ihr has no umlaut, and du ends in -st anyway because the stem already ends in s.

example.de: Ihr lasst das Essen liefern, und du lässt es auch liefern.
example.en: You all have the food delivered, and you have it delivered too.

cards.more: A quick way to remember: lassen behaves like fahren, schlafen and tragen, the verbs that put two dots on the a for du and er. Say them in a row: du fährst, du schläfst, du lässt. Er fährt, er schläft, er lässt. A typical mistake is Er lasst, which sounds almost the same but is wrong in writing. The two dots belong only to du and er/sie/es. For ich, wir, ihr, sie and Sie you just take the stem lass- and the normal ending.

cards.title: Word order: lassen in position 2, the infinitive at the end
cards.body: lassen builds the same frame as a modal verb. lassen stands in position 2, the infinitive closes the sentence. Everything else goes in the middle: the thing, the time, the place. Time comes before place, as always.
cards.lead: You know all forms of lassen now. Next comes the order of the words, which is the same frame as with müssen or können.

examples.de: Leon lässt sein Fahrrad im Laden reparieren.
examples.en: Leon is having his bike repaired at the shop.

examples.de: Lässt du die Jacke reinigen?
examples.en: Are you having the jacket cleaned?

examples.de: Ich lasse heute meine Haare schneiden.
examples.en: I am having my hair cut today.

deeper.text: If the time or another word stands in position 1, lassen still stays in position 2 and the subject moves right behind it: Am Freitag lässt Mira ihre Haare schneiden. You can also combine lassen with a modal verb. Then the modal is in position 2 and both infinitives go to the end, lassen last: Leon will sein Fahrrad reparieren lassen.

example.de: Am Freitag lässt Mira ihre Haare schneiden.
example.en: On Friday Mira is having her hair cut.

cards.more: Picture a sandwich. The two slices of bread are lassen and the infinitive. Everything you want to say goes between them: what, when, where. Mira lässt am Freitag ihre Haare schneiden. Leon lässt sein Fahrrad im Laden reparieren. English keeps the words close together (have the bike repaired), but German opens the sandwich wide. When you speak, say lassen early, then collect the details, and only close with the infinitive when you are done.

cards.title: Questions and no: Lässt du …? and nicht
cards.body: In a yes/no question lassen goes to position 1: Lässt du das Fahrrad reparieren? To say no, put nicht right before the infinitive at the end: Ich lasse das Fahrrad nicht reparieren. Often you add what you do instead: ich kaufe ein neues.
cards.lead: You can build statements with lassen. Now you turn them into questions and say no, with one fixed place for nicht.

examples.de: Ich lasse das Fahrrad nicht reparieren, ich kaufe ein neues.
examples.en: I am not having the bike repaired, I am buying a new one.

examples.de: Wo lässt du deine Haare schneiden?
examples.en: Where do you get your hair cut?

examples.de: Anna lässt ihre Bilder nicht im Laden rahmen.
examples.en: Anna is not having her pictures framed at the shop.

deeper.text: nicht before the infinitive says no to the whole idea. If you only want to say no to one detail, nicht moves in front of that detail and you usually add sondern: Anna lässt ihre Bilder nicht im Laden rahmen, sondern bei einer Freundin. Here she still has them framed, just not in the shop. The same rule works with modal verbs, so nothing new to learn.

example.de: Ich lasse die Jacke nicht heute reinigen, sondern morgen.
example.en: I am not having the jacket cleaned today, but tomorrow.

cards.more: Think of a shop assistant who asks you questions. Lassen Sie das Fahrrad hier? Lässt du es heute reparieren? Each question starts with the verb, the infinitive still waits at the end. Now imagine you say no. The infinitive is the action, so nicht stands right in front of it, like a stop sign before the action: nicht reparieren, nicht schneiden. With a question word like wo or wann, lassen moves back to position 2: Wo lässt du deine Haare schneiden?

cards.title: Mini dialogue: Das ist ja praktisch!
cards.body: Leon comes home. Mira asks about the bike. Read the six lines and find every lassen and every infinitive at the end. Notice Mira's little ja: it shows surprise and agreement, not the answer yes.
cards.lead: Now all pieces come together: Leon's bike, the forms of lassen and the word order. Read how Leon and Mira talk about it in the WG kitchen.

examples.de: Ich lasse die Bremsen reparieren.
examples.en: I am having the brakes repaired.

examples.de: Das ist ja praktisch!
examples.en: That is really handy!

examples.de: Lässt du auch den Platten reparieren?
examples.en: Are you having the flat tyre fixed too?

deeper.text: The particle ja is everywhere in spoken German and is never stressed. Das ist ja praktisch means: I see it now and I agree, that is handy. Das ist ja teuer! shows surprise, often a little negative. If you stress ja, it becomes the answer yes, so keep it short and quiet. Doch and mal are similar small words that add feeling, not information.

example.de: 45 Euro? Das ist ja teuer!
example.en: 45 euros? That is really expensive!

cards.more: Read the dialogue aloud and act both people. Mira is curious, Leon is a bit proud of his solution. When Leon says Ich lasse die Bremsen reparieren, stress reparieren at the end. When Mira says Das ist ja praktisch, say ja quickly and softly, and put the energy on praktisch. That melody makes you sound natural. Then change one detail and play it again: a jacket at the cleaner's instead of the bike, or a pizza from a delivery service.
steps: Mira: Wo ist dein Fahrrad?
Leon: Im Laden um die Ecke. Ich lasse die Bremsen reparieren.
Mira: Und den Platten?
Leon: Den auch. Ich habe kein Werkzeug. Das kostet 45 Euro.
Mira: Und wann ist es fertig?
Leon: Morgen. Das ist ja praktisch, oder? – Mira: Ja, das ist ja wirklich praktisch!

Ich lasse das Fahrrad nicht reparieren.

blind.hint: Ben + lassen (er-form) + die Pizza + infinitive at the end.

Mein Fahrrad hat einen Platten, und die Bremse funktioniert nicht. Ich habe kein Werkzeug. Ich lasse es im Fahrradladen reparieren.

lessons.title: Lass mich helfen!: lassen = let, allow, leave
lessons.goal: Say what someone allows and what you leave somewhere, offer help with Lass mich …! and use lassen at the end of weil-, dass- and wenn-clauses.

grammar.topic: lassen = let / leave; lassen in subordinate clauses
grammar.point: lassen + person + infinitive means let: Herr Ali lässt Leon kochen. lassen without an infinitive means leave: Ich lasse das Handy zu Hause. Imperative: Lass …! / Lasst …! / Lassen Sie …! After weil, dass and wenn the infinitive comes first and lassen is the very last word.
grammar.oneLine: Leon ist froh, weil Herr Ali ihn kochen lässt.

mistake.wrong: Leon ist froh, weil Herr Ali lässt ihn kochen.
mistake.right: Leon ist froh, weil Herr Ali ihn kochen lässt.
mistake.why: After weil the finite verb goes to the end. With lassen the infinitive comes first and lassen is the very last word.

terms.meaning: the person after lassen does the action, because you allow it
no infinitive: something stays where it is
the form for requests and offers: Lass mich helfen!

cards.title: Before we start: one verb, three jobs
cards.body: Yesterday Leon had his bike repaired. lassen can do more. On Saturdays Leon helps in the kitchen of „Zum Löwen“, and Herr Ali lets him cook. And when Leon goes to work, he leaves his phone at home. German uses lassen for all three ideas: have done, let and leave.
steps: You already know: Leon lässt sein Fahrrad reparieren. A service does the work, Leon organises it.
New today: Herr Ali lässt Leon in der Küche helfen (he lets him). Ich lasse das Handy zu Hause (I leave it). And lassen in weil- and dass-clauses goes to the very end.
By the end you can: say what someone allows, what you leave somewhere, ask with Lass mich …! and use lassen after weil and dass.

examples.de: Leon lässt sein Fahrrad reparieren.
examples.en: Leon is having his bike repaired.
examples.why: You know this: a service does the work.

examples.de: Herr Ali lässt Leon in der Küche helfen.
examples.en: Herr Ali lets Leon help in the kitchen.
examples.why: New today: the person after lassen does the action.

cards.more: Think of lassen as a door. Yesterday you opened the door for a service: Ich lasse das Fahrrad reparieren. Today the door opens for a person you allow in: Herr Ali lässt Leon kochen. And sometimes the door simply stays as it is: you leave something where it is, Ich lasse das Handy zu Hause. Same verb, same forms (du lässt, er lässt), but three jobs. The trick of today is to ask one question: who does the work?

cards.title: lassen = let, allow
cards.body: lassen can also mean let or allow. Then a person comes after lassen, and this person does the action of the infinitive. Herr Ali lets Leon help: Leon helps. With nicht, lassen means not allow. The frame stays the same: lassen in position 2, infinitive at the end.
cards.lead: Yesterday a service did the work after lassen. Now a person you allow does it: same frame, new meaning.

examples.de: Herr Ali lässt Leon samstags in der Küche helfen.
examples.en: Herr Ali lets Leon help in the kitchen on Saturdays.

examples.de: Frau Weber lässt die Katze nicht in die Küche.
examples.en: Frau Weber does not let the cat into the kitchen.

examples.de: Lässt du mich mal fahren?
examples.en: Will you let me drive for once?

deeper.text: The person after lassen is in the accusative: Herr Ali lässt ihn kochen, lässt mich fahren, lässt uns spielen. Compare erlauben, which also means allow but works differently: it takes the dative and a zu-part. Herr Ali erlaubt ihm, die Suppe zu kochen. So lassen is the short, everyday way, erlauben sounds more official.

example.de: Herr Ali erlaubt ihm, die Suppe zu kochen.
example.en: Herr Ali allows him to cook the soup.

cards.more: English has a twin for this meaning: let. Herr Ali lets Leon help, Herr Ali lässt Leon helfen. Both languages put the person right after the verb and use the plain infinitive, without to. So here English helps you. Only the position of the infinitive is different: in German it waits at the end. Picture Herr Ali opening the kitchen door and waving Leon in. With nicht the door stays closed, like for Frau Weber's cat.

cards.title: Have done or let? Ask: who does the work?
cards.body: Both meanings look the same. Ask one question: who does the work? If a service or someone you pay does it, lassen means have done. If the person right after lassen does it, because you allow it, lassen means let.
cards.lead: Now you know two meanings of lassen with the same form. This card gives you one question to tell them apart in every sentence.

examples.de: Anna lässt ihr Bild rahmen.
examples.en: Anna has her picture framed.
examples.why: A shop does the work: have done.

examples.de: Anna lässt Ben ihr Bild sehen.
examples.en: Anna lets Ben see her picture.
examples.why: Ben sees it, Anna allows it: let.

examples.de: Ich lasse dich gewinnen.
examples.en: I let you win.
examples.why: You win: let.

deeper.text: Sometimes only the context decides. Ich lasse das Kind malen can mean I let the child paint (it wants to), or with a little help, I have the child paint (I tell it to). In real life the situation makes it clear. A good tip: if the thing after lassen cannot act, like a bike or a picture, it is always have done.

example.de: Ich lasse die Kinder im Garten spielen.
example.en: I let the children play in the garden.

cards.more: Imagine two cameras. The first camera films the shop: a person frames Anna's picture, and Anna is not even there. That is have done. The second camera films the living room: Ben stands in front of the picture and looks at it, and Anna smiles and allows it. That is let. In your head, turn on the camera and look who is moving. A thing like das Bild cannot do anything, so a sentence with only a thing is always have done.

rows: Anna lässt Ben ihr Bild sehen.

cards.title: lassen = leave (no infinitive)
cards.body: With no infinitive at the end, lassen means leave: something stays where it is. Ich lasse das Handy zu Hause. The place is important. anlassen means leave on (a light, a machine), separable like anmachen: Ben lässt das Licht an.
cards.lead: Two meanings had an infinitive at the end. The third one has none: lassen alone means leave something somewhere.

examples.de: Ich lasse das Handy zu Hause.
examples.en: I leave my phone at home.

examples.de: Lass die Tasche hier!
examples.en: Leave the bag here!

examples.de: Ben lässt das Licht an.
examples.en: Ben leaves the light on.

deeper.text: A very useful fixed phrase is jemanden in Ruhe lassen, to leave someone alone. Lass mich in Ruhe! is strong, even rude, so say it only when you are really annoyed. Friendlier: Lass ihn bitte in Ruhe, er muss lernen. Another one is liegen lassen, to leave something behind by mistake: Ich habe meinen Schlüssel liegen lassen. Here you only need to recognise it.

example.de: Lass Mira bitte in Ruhe, sie muss lernen.
example.en: Please leave Mira alone, she has to study.

cards.more: Look at the end of the sentence. If an infinitive is waiting there, lassen means have done or let. If the sentence ends with a place, like zu Hause or hier, or with the little word an, lassen means leave. English uses leave in exactly the same way: leave the phone at home, leave the light on. A quick test: can you translate with leave and it sounds right? Then you need no infinitive at all.

rows: Ich lasse das Handy zu Hause.

cards.title: Lass mich helfen! The imperative of lassen
cards.body: To offer help or ask for a turn, use the imperative: Lass mich helfen! (du), Lasst mich helfen! (ihr), Lassen Sie mich helfen! (Sie). The du-form has no umlaut and no ending. Lass das! is short and means stop that.
cards.lead: You can use lassen in statements and questions. Now you use it to offer help politely, with the three imperative forms.

examples.de: Lass mich das machen!
examples.en: Let me do that!

examples.de: Lassen Sie mich das tragen, Frau Weber!
examples.en: Let me carry that, Frau Weber!

examples.de: Lass das!
examples.en: Stop that!

deeper.text: With uns, the imperative means let's: Lass uns gehen! (to one friend) or Lasst uns gehen! (to several friends). It sounds a bit more personal than Gehen wir!, which means the same. You only need to recognise it for now. Careful: Lass uns in Ruhe means leave us alone, so the meaning depends on the rest of the sentence.

example.de: Lass uns ins Kino gehen!
example.en: Let's go to the cinema!

cards.more: Think of a real scene: Frau Weber carries a heavy box up the stairs. Leon comes along and says: Lassen Sie mich das tragen! That is polite and kind, perfect for the neighbour. To Mira he would say Lass mich das tragen! Now a different scene: Ben plays with the light switch, on, off, on, off. Mira gets annoyed: Lass das! Two words, and everybody understands. The du-form is just lass, the stem, like komm or geh.

cards.title: lassen at the very end: weil, dass, wenn
cards.body: After weil, dass or wenn the finite verb goes to the end. With lassen there are two verbs at the end: first the infinitive, then lassen as the very last word. Leon ist froh, weil Herr Ali ihn kochen lässt.
cards.lead: You know that weil and dass send the verb to the end. With lassen two verbs meet there, so this card shows their fixed order.

examples.de: Leon ist froh, weil Herr Ali ihn kochen lässt.
examples.en: Leon is glad because Herr Ali lets him cook.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass Mira ihre Haare schneiden lässt.
examples.en: I think that Mira is having her hair cut.

examples.de: Wenn du das Fahrrad reparieren lässt, kostet es 45 Euro.
examples.en: If you have the bike repaired, it costs 45 euros.

deeper.text: In the Perfekt, lassen does something strange. With an infinitive you do not say gelassen, but use lassen twice as an infinitive: Ich habe das Fahrrad reparieren lassen. This is called the double infinitive. Gelassen appears only when lassen means leave: Ich habe das Handy zu Hause gelassen. Just recognise this form for now.

example.de: Ich habe das Fahrrad reparieren lassen.
example.en: I had the bike repaired.

cards.more: Build it like a train in five cars. Car 1: the conjunction (weil). Car 2: the subject (Herr Ali). Car 3: the middle (ihn). Car 4: the infinitive (kochen). Car 5, always last: lassen (lässt). The main sentence before the comma stays normal. A typical mistake is to keep lässt in position 2 after weil, as in weil Herr Ali lässt ihn kochen. That is how people talk in some regions, but in writing and in the exam, lassen must close the clause.
steps: 1 conjunction: weil
2 subject: Herr Ali
3 middle: ihn
4 infinitive: kochen
5 lassen, last: lässt.

cards.title: Mini dialogue in „Zum Löwen“
cards.body: Saturday in Herr Ali's restaurant. Leon wants to cook the soup. Read the six lines and find the three meanings of lassen and the imperative. Leon says Sie to Herr Ali, Herr Ali says du to Leon.
cards.lead: All meanings of lassen meet in one real scene. Read how Leon asks for permission in the kitchen of „Zum Löwen“.

examples.de: Darf ich heute die Suppe kochen?
examples.en: May I cook the soup today?

examples.de: Ich lasse dich die Suppe kochen.
examples.en: I will let you cook the soup.

examples.de: Lassen Sie mich mal abschmecken!
examples.en: Let me have a taste!

deeper.text: Leon asks with darf ich, and Herr Ali answers with lassen. That is a natural pair: dürfen asks for permission, lassen gives it. A boss or parent can also say Ich lasse dich das machen, wenn …, which adds a condition. In a restaurant kitchen you also hear die Aushilfe, a helper who works a few hours, like Leon on Saturdays.

example.de: Leon ist samstags die Aushilfe in der Küche.
example.en: Leon is the kitchen helper on Saturdays.

cards.more: Read the dialogue twice, once as Leon and once as Herr Ali. As Leon you are polite and a little nervous: Darf ich …? Lassen Sie mich …! As Herr Ali you are friendly but strict: Ich lasse dich …, wenn … Then look for the three jobs of lassen: let (Ich lasse dich kochen), leave (Lass das Salz noch hier) and the imperative (Lassen Sie mich …!). Mark each one with a different colour in your head.
steps: Leon: Herr Ali, darf ich heute die Suppe kochen?
Herr Ali: Ich lasse dich die Suppe kochen, wenn du zuerst das Gemüse schneidest.
Leon: Gern! Und das Salz?
Herr Ali: Lass das Salz noch hier. Erst rühren, dann kommt das Salz.
Leon: Fertig! Lassen Sie mich mal abschmecken!
Herr Ali: Ich bin froh, dass ich dich kochen lasse. Sehr gut!

drills.prompt: Anna lässt Ben ihr Bild sehen. Who sees the picture?
drills.hint: The person after lassen does the action.
drills.explanation: lassen = let: Ben sees the picture, Anna allows it.

drills.prompt: Which sentence means: I leave my phone at home?
options: Ich lasse dich das Handy sehen.
Ich lasse das Handy zu Hause.
drills.hint: leave: no infinitive, a place at the end.
drills.explanation: Ich lasse das Handy zu Hause.

drills.hint: du-imperative: the stem, no ending, no umlaut.
drills.explanation: Lass mich helfen, Mira!

drills.prompt: ___ Sie mich das tragen, Frau Weber! (imperative, Sie)
drills.hint: Polite imperative: the verb first, then Sie.
drills.explanation: Lassen Sie mich das tragen, Frau Weber!

drills.prompt: Put in order: Leon ist froh, weil … (Herr Ali lets him cook).
drills.hint: Conjunction, subject, middle, infinitive, lassen last.
drills.explanation: Leon ist froh, weil Herr Ali ihn kochen lässt.

drills.prompt: Ich glaube, dass Mira ihre Haare ___.
drills.hint: Two verbs at the end: which one is last?
drills.explanation: …, dass Mira ihre Haare schneiden lässt.

blind.prompt: Write in German: Frau Weber does not let the cat into the kitchen.
answers: Frau Weber lässt die Katze nicht in die Küche.
blind.hint: lassen = let; nicht before the place; in die Küche (direction).
blind.explanation: Frau Weber lässt die Katze nicht in die Küche.

check.hint: Who cooks?
check.explanation: Leon cooks, Herr Ali allows it: lassen = let.

check.explanation: A service repairs it: lassen = have done.

check.explanation: Wenn du das Fahrrad reparieren lässt, kostet es 45 Euro.

check.hint: ihr-imperative: like the ihr-form, without ihr.
check.explanation: Lasst die Tasche hier, Leon und Mira!

check.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Ich glaube, dass Anna lässt ihr Bild rahmen.
Ich glaube, dass Anna ihr Bild rahmen lässt.
Ich glaube, dass Anna ihr Bild lässt rahmen.
check.hint: After dass: infinitive, then lassen at the very end.
check.explanation: …, dass Anna ihr Bild rahmen lässt.

check.hint: Short and means stop that.

lessons.title: Online oder im Laden?: buying habits and services
lessons.goal: Talk about your buying habits and the services you use, say how often, and give reasons with weil, da and obwohl, with lassen at the end.

grammar.point: No new grammar: use lassen in all three meanings and give reasons. weil and da give a normal reason, obwohl an unexpected one; all three send the verb to the end. With lassen the infinitive comes first and lassen is last: …, weil ich das Essen liefern lasse.
grammar.oneLine: Ich lasse das Essen liefern, weil ich keine Zeit habe.

mistake.wrong: Ich lasse das Essen liefern, weil ich habe keine Zeit.
mistake.right: Ich lasse das Essen liefern, weil ich keine Zeit habe.
mistake.why: weil sends the finite verb to the very end of its clause.

terms.meaning: a word that says how often: immer, oft, selten, nie
although: introduces an unexpected reason, verb at the end
a Berlin word for your own small neighbourhood

cards.title: Before we start: what do you do yourself, what do you let others do?
cards.body: No new grammar today. You use what you have: lassen in all its jobs, and weil, da and obwohl. The topic is shopping. Ben buys almost everything online at TechnoMax. Anna prefers the small shops in her Kiez. Who is right? Today you talk about your own buying habits and give reasons.
steps: You already know: Ich lasse die Pizza liefern. Ich kaufe online, weil es schnell geht.
New today: words for online shopping and shops, and longer reasons: Anna kauft lieber im Laden, obwohl es teurer ist.
By the end you can: describe how and how often you buy things, and say why, with lassen at the end of a weil-clause.

examples.de: Ich lasse die Pizza liefern.
examples.en: I have the pizza delivered.
examples.why: Lesson 1: have done.

examples.de: Anna kauft lieber im Laden, obwohl es teurer ist.
examples.en: Anna prefers to buy in the shop, although it is more expensive.
examples.why: Today: an unexpected reason with obwohl.

cards.more: Think about your last purchase. Did you click on a button and wait for a parcel, or did you walk into a shop and talk to a person? Both have good sides. Online is fast and you can compare prices at home. In a shop someone advises you and you can try things on. Today you collect the words for both worlds, and you practise reasons: weil and da for normal reasons, obwohl for a surprise. And lassen comes back at the end of those clauses.

cards.title: Buying words: online or in the shop
cards.body: Online you order, the shop delivers, you wait for the delivery time and sometimes pay shipping costs. If something is wrong, you send it back. In a shop you try things on, a salesperson advises you, and you can pay cash.
cards.lead: Before Ben and Anna can argue, you need the words of both worlds. This card sorts them into online and in the shop.

examples.de: Der Versand ist bei TechnoMax kostenlos.
examples.en: Shipping is free at TechnoMax.

examples.de: Die Jacke passt nicht, ich schicke sie zurück.
examples.en: The jacket does not fit, I am sending it back.

examples.de: Im Laden kann ich die Schuhe anprobieren.
examples.en: In the shop I can try on the shoes.

deeper.text: Die Versandkosten is a plural-only word, like die Leute or die Kosten, so the verb is always plural: Die Versandkosten sind hoch. Zurückschicken and anprobieren are separable: Ich schicke die Jacke zurück. In a shop you can also say Kann ich mit Karte bezahlen? Many small shops in Germany still prefer cash, so people often ask before they buy.

example.de: Kann ich hier mit Karte bezahlen?
example.en: Can I pay by card here?

cards.more: Imagine two shopping baskets. In the online basket: bestellen, liefern, die Lieferzeit, die Versandkosten, zurückschicken. You sit at home in comfort, but you wait and you cannot touch anything. In the shop basket: anprobieren, beraten, die Beratung, bar bezahlen. You go out, maybe it rains, but you can feel the jacket and ask questions. When you learn a new word today, put it in one of the two baskets in your head.

cards.title: Ben and Anna: two buying types
cards.body: Ben orders at TechnoMax because it is fast and cheap. Anna buys in her Kiez, the neighbourhood, because she knows the people and gets good advice. Use comparatives to compare: billiger, schneller, bequemer, persönlicher.
cards.lead: Now you have the words. Here are two people who use them in very different ways: Ben online and Anna in her Kiez.

examples.de: Ben bestellt bei TechnoMax, weil es schnell geht.
examples.en: Ben orders at TechnoMax because it is quick.

examples.de: Anna kauft im Kiez, da sie die Leute kennt.
examples.en: Anna buys in her neighbourhood since she knows the people.

examples.de: Im Laden ist es persönlicher als online.
examples.en: In the shop it is more personal than online.

deeper.text: Der Kiez is a typical Berlin word for one's own small neighbourhood, with its bakery, little shops and familiar faces. In Hamburg or Munich people say das Viertel instead. Berliners are proud of their Kiez, so the word is warm and personal. Small shop owners are called Händler, and many of them live in the same Kiez as their customers.

example.de: In meinem Kiez kenne ich alle Händler.
example.en: In my neighbourhood I know all the shopkeepers.

cards.more: Read both profiles like a dating app. Ben: likes speed, low prices, sofa, clicks at midnight. Anna: likes chatting, advice, fresh bread, knows the baker by name. Neither of them is wrong. The comparatives tell you why they choose: for Ben online is schneller and billiger, for Anna the shop is persönlicher. When you talk about yourself, choose one comparative that fits your life and add a weil-clause. That is already a good B1 answer.

cards.title: How often? Habits with immer, oft, selten, nie
cards.body: To describe habits, use frequency words: immer, meistens, oft, manchmal, selten, nie. They usually stand right after the verb, or in position 1 for emphasis. With lassen they come before the thing: Ich lasse selten Essen liefern.
cards.lead: Ben and Anna have clear habits. To describe your own, you need words for how often, and they fit well with lassen.

examples.de: Ich bestelle selten online.
examples.en: I rarely order online.

examples.de: Ben lässt fast immer das Essen liefern.
examples.en: Ben almost always has the food delivered.

examples.de: Manchmal kauft Anna auch im Internet.
examples.en: Sometimes Anna also buys on the internet.

deeper.text: fast (almost) makes a frequency word softer and sounds very natural: fast immer, fast nie. Germans also like ab und zu, which means now and then and is a little less than manchmal. For a habit in a time frame use pro or im: zweimal pro Woche, einmal im Monat. These fit at the same place in the sentence as oft.

example.de: Ich bestelle ab und zu online, vielleicht einmal im Monat.
example.en: I order online now and then, maybe once a month.

cards.more: Draw a line from 100 to 0 in your head. At 100 stands immer, at 0 stands nie. In between, from left to right: meistens, oft, manchmal, selten. Now place yourself on the line for different things: online shopping, food delivery, the hairdresser. Ich lasse oft Essen liefern, but ich kaufe nie Kleidung online. A short honest sentence about your life sticks better than any table, so say three of them aloud right now.
steps: immer (100 %)
meistens
oft
manchmal
selten
nie (0 %)

cards.title: Services in the Kiez: who does what?
cards.body: Many jobs in everyday life go to a service. Name the place, say who works there, and build a lassen sentence: Im Fahrradladen lasse ich mein Fahrrad reparieren. This is how you talk about the services you use.
cards.lead: From buying things we go to buying work. The services from lesson 1 come back here, each with its own lassen sentence.

examples.de: In der Reinigung lasse ich meinen Mantel reinigen.
examples.en: At the dry cleaner's I have my coat cleaned.

examples.de: Beim Friseur lässt Mira ihre Haare schneiden.
examples.en: At the hairdresser's Mira has her hair cut.

examples.de: Bei der Schneiderin lässt Anna eine Hose kürzen.
examples.en: At the tailor's Anna has some trousers shortened.

deeper.text: Notice the prepositions. For a shop or place you use in: in der Reinigung, im Fahrradladen. For a person you use bei: beim Friseur, bei der Schneiderin. To say where you take something, use the accusative with in or zu with the dative: Ich bringe den Mantel in die Reinigung. Ich gehe zum Friseur.

example.de: Ich bringe den Mantel in die Reinigung.
example.en: I take the coat to the dry cleaner's.

cards.more: Take a walk through Anna's Kiez. On the corner is the bike shop, where Leon leaves his bike. Next door is the dry cleaner's with coats in the window. Across the street the hairdresser, where Mira sits every six weeks. Upstairs the tailor, who shortens Anna's trousers. And on the road the bikes of the delivery service rush past with Ben's dinner. Each stop is one lassen sentence. Walk the street in your head and say them in order.

cards.title: Reasons: weil, da and obwohl with lassen
cards.body: Give a normal reason with weil or da, an unexpected one with obwohl. All three send the verb to the end. With lassen, the infinitive comes first and lassen is last. If the clause starts the sentence, the main verb follows right after the comma.
cards.lead: You can name services now. To defend your choices you need reasons, and lassen must find its place at the end of them.

examples.de: Ich lasse das Essen liefern, weil ich keine Zeit habe.
examples.en: I have the food delivered because I have no time.

examples.de: Obwohl es teuer ist, lasse ich meine Jacke reinigen.
examples.en: Although it is expensive, I have my jacket cleaned.

examples.de: Da Ben keine Zeit hat, lässt er das Paket in den Laden liefern.
examples.en: Since Ben has no time, he has the parcel delivered to the shop.

deeper.text: da and weil are almost the same, but da likes position 1 and gives a reason that the listener already knows or accepts: Da es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause. weil gives new information and is the only one that answers a warum-question: Warum? Weil ich keine Zeit habe. You would never answer a question with da alone.

example.de: Warum bestellst du online? – Weil es schneller geht.
example.en: Why do you order online? – Because it is quicker.

cards.more: Think of reasons as two kinds of arrows. A weil or da arrow points straight: no time, so delivery. An obwohl arrow makes a curve: it is expensive, but I do it anyway. Choose the arrow by asking: is the result what you expect? Then count the verbs at the end. Weil ich keine Zeit habe has one. Weil ich das Essen liefern lasse has two, and lassen is always last. Practise both arrows with your own habits.

cards.title: Interview: Wie kaufen Sie ein?
cards.body: Leon does a survey for the university and interviews Frau Weber. He says Sie to her, she says du to him. Read the eight lines and find the frequency words, the reasons and lassen.
cards.lead: Everything from today in one real conversation: buying words, how often, services and reasons. Leon asks Frau Weber about her buying habits.

examples.de: Wie oft kaufen Sie online ein?
examples.en: How often do you shop online?

examples.de: Ich kaufe fast nie online.
examples.en: I almost never buy online.

examples.de: Ich lasse nur meine Bücher liefern, weil sie so schwer sind.
examples.en: I only have my books delivered because they are so heavy.

deeper.text: A survey is eine Umfrage, and the people who answer are die Befragten. In a polite interview Germans often start with a short softener: Darf ich Ihnen ein paar Fragen stellen? At the end they thank with Vielen Dank für das Gespräch. These two phrases frame any interview, from a uni project to a job talk.

example.de: Darf ich Ihnen ein paar Fragen stellen?
example.en: May I ask you a few questions?

cards.more: Play the interview with a partner or alone with two voices. Leon is polite and a bit formal: Sie, Ihnen, Darf ich …? Frau Weber is friendly and talks to him like a neighbour: du. Then turn it around: Frau Weber interviews you. Answer with your own habits, a frequency word and one reason with weil or obwohl. Change only the answers, keep the questions. After three rounds the questions will feel like your own.
steps: Leon: Frau Weber, darf ich Ihnen ein paar Fragen für eine Umfrage stellen?
Frau Weber: Natürlich, Leon. Frag nur!
Leon: Wie oft kaufen Sie online ein?
Frau Weber: Fast nie. Ich gehe lieber in die Läden im Kiez, weil man mich dort gut berät.
Leon: Und lassen Sie manchmal etwas liefern?
Frau Weber: Nur meine Bücher, weil sie so schwer sind. Und du?
Leon: Ich bestelle oft online, obwohl die Lieferzeit manchmal lang ist.
Frau Weber: Na ja, jeder hat sein Kaufverhalten. Viel Erfolg mit der Umfrage!

drills.hint: What do you pay when a parcel comes to you?

drills.hint: Expensive, but she still buys there: an unexpected reason.

drills.hint: Infinitive first, then lassen at the very end.
drills.explanation: …, weil Ben das Essen liefern lässt.

drills.prompt: Ich bestelle ___ online: nur einmal im Jahr.
drills.hint: Once a year is not much.
drills.explanation: selten = rarely.

drills.prompt: Obwohl es teuer ist, ___ ich meine Jacke reinigen. (have done)
drills.hint: After the obwohl-part the main verb comes first; ich-form.
drills.explanation: Obwohl es teuer ist, lasse ich meine Jacke reinigen.

blind.prompt: Write in German: I rarely order online because the shipping costs are high.

lessons.title: Robbi ist kaputt. Deshalb …: deshalb, deswegen, darum, daher
lessons.goal: Say what follows from a problem with deshalb, deswegen, darum and daher, in position 1 or after the verb, and tell darum as a result word from darum as a da-word.

grammar.topic: Result words: deshalb, deswegen, darum, daher
grammar.point: deshalb, deswegen, darum and daher all mean 'that's why' and introduce the result (Folge). In position 1 the verb comes right after them, then the subject: Darum funktioniert Robbi nicht. They can also stand in the middle after the verb: Ben schickt Robbi deshalb zurück. A second verb part stays at the end. weil gives the cause and sends the verb to the end. daher is a bit more formal.
grammar.oneLine: Der Akku ist leer. Darum funktioniert Robbi nicht.

mistake.wrong: Der Akku ist leer, deshalb Robbi funktioniert nicht.
mistake.right: Der Akku ist leer, deshalb funktioniert Robbi nicht.
mistake.why: deshalb takes position 1 of its sentence, so the verb must come right after it. The subject moves behind the verb.

terms.meaning: a word like deshalb or darum that says what follows: 'that's why'
cause / result: weil gives the Ursache, deshalb gives the Folge
da(r) + preposition (darum, darauf) standing for a thing after a verb with a preposition

cards.title: Before we start: from 'deshalb' to three new friends
cards.body: Things break. When they do, you need to say what follows: the battery is empty, that's why the robot stops. You already know deshalb from A2 chapter 9 and weil and da from B1 chapter 1. Today you meet three more words for 'that's why': deswegen, darum and daher. And you meet Ben's new robot vacuum, Robbi.
steps: You already know: deshalb in position 1 from A2 chapter 9 (Ich bin müde. Deshalb gehe ich nach Hause.) and weil/da with the verb at the end from B1 chapter 1.
New today: deswegen, darum and daher. They mean the same as deshalb and follow the same word order.
By the end you can: tell Ben's Robbi story and say what follows from each problem in two or three different ways.

examples.de: Ich bin müde. Deshalb gehe ich nach Hause.
examples.en: I'm tired. That's why I'm going home.
examples.why: You know this already.

examples.de: Robbi ist laut. Darum kann niemand schlafen.
examples.en: Robbi is loud. That's why nobody can sleep.
examples.why: New today: darum works exactly like deshalb.

cards.more: Think of a row of dominoes. The first one falls: Robbi is loud. The next one falls because of it: nobody can sleep. German has a little family of words that point from the first domino to the next one: deshalb, deswegen, darum, daher. You already own one of them. Today you collect the rest, see where they sit in the sentence, and learn one trap with darum. We go step by step, one card at a time, with Ben's broken robot as our story.

cards.title: Meet Robbi: Ben's new robot vacuum
cards.body: Ben has ordered a Saugroboter (robot vacuum) from the online shop TechnoMax: 299 Euro, two years Garantie (guarantee). The robot's name is Robbi. After one week there are problems: Robbi is loud, he bumps into the walls and the Akku is leer (empty) after ten minutes. Robbi is defekt (faulty).
cards.lead: Before we learn the new 'that's why' words, we need a story full of problems. This card introduces Robbi, the robot vacuum that will give Ben a lot of trouble today.

examples.de: Ben hat Robbi bei TechnoMax bestellt.
examples.en: Ben ordered Robbi from TechnoMax.

examples.de: Robbi stößt gegen die Wand.
examples.en: Robbi bumps into the wall.

examples.de: Der Akku ist nach zehn Minuten leer.
examples.en: The battery is empty after ten minutes.

deeper.text: Saugroboter is a compound noun: saugen (to vacuum, literally to suck) plus Roboter. In a German compound the LAST word decides the gender, so der Roboter gives der Saugroboter. The plural does not change at the end: ein Saugroboter, zwei Saugroboter. Many words in this story work like that: die Lade + die Station gives die Ladestation, where Robbi charges.

example.de: Robbi fährt zurück zur Ladestation.
example.en: Robbi drives back to the charging station.

cards.more: Picture Ben's living room. A round, flat robot rolls over the floor and is supposed to clean on its own while Ben is at work. Ben is happy: he unpacks it, switches it on and goes out. But when he comes home, Robbi is standing in a corner, silent, with an empty battery. Yesterday it was so noisy that nobody in the WG could relax. Every problem has a consequence, and that is exactly what today's words are for.
steps: bestellt: Ben hat Robbi bei TechnoMax bestellt (299 Euro, zwei Jahre Garantie).
geliefert: Das Paket ist nach zwei Tagen gekommen.
ausgepackt: Ben hat Robbi ausgepackt und eingeschaltet.
Problem: Robbi ist laut, stößt gegen die Wände, und der Akku ist schnell leer.

cards.title: Reason or result?
cards.body: Two directions. weil (and da) gives the Ursache (cause): the verb goes to the END. deshalb gives the Folge (result): the verb comes RIGHT AFTER it. Same story, two ways: Ben ist wütend, weil Robbi defekt ist. / Robbi ist defekt. Deshalb ist Ben wütend.
cards.lead: Now that you know Robbi's problems, this card shows the two directions of one story: the cause with weil, and the result with deshalb.

examples.de: Ben ist wütend, weil Robbi defekt ist.
examples.en: Ben is angry because Robbi is faulty.
examples.why: weil: the cause, verb at the end.

examples.de: Robbi ist defekt. Deshalb ist Ben wütend.
examples.en: Robbi is faulty. That's why Ben is angry.
examples.why: deshalb: the result, verb next.

examples.de: Weil der Akku leer ist, fährt Robbi nicht mehr.
examples.en: Because the battery is empty, Robbi stops driving.

deeper.text: There is a third way you know from A1: denn. It also gives the cause, but it sits in position 0, so it does not move the verb at all. Robbi fährt nicht mehr, denn der Akku ist leer. Compare: weil pushes the verb to the end, deshalb pulls it straight after itself, denn leaves it alone. Three little words, three different effects on the verb.

example.de: Robbi fährt nicht mehr, denn der Akku ist leer.
example.en: Robbi isn't driving any more, because the battery is empty.

cards.more: Imagine an arrow from left to right: Ursache → Folge. With weil you stand on the right side and look back: why is Ben angry? Because Robbi is faulty. With deshalb you stand on the left side and look forward: Robbi is faulty, so what happens next? Ben gets angry. Quick test for yourself: ask 'why?' and you need weil. Ask 'and so?' and you need deshalb. The facts stay the same; only the direction of your arrow changes.

cards.title: Four words, one meaning
cards.body: deshalb, deswegen, darum and daher all mean 'that's why' or 'so'. They give the result and they all work the same way: verb right after them. In speaking, all four are fine. daher sounds a bit more formal, so it fits well in an e-mail or a letter. darum and deswegen are very common in everyday talk.
cards.lead: You can now say a result with deshalb. This card adds three words that do the same job, so you can vary your sentences and choose the right tone.

examples.de: Der Akku ist leer. Darum funktioniert Robbi nicht.
examples.en: The battery is empty. That's why Robbi doesn't work.

examples.de: Das Gerät ist defekt. Daher möchte ich es zurückschicken.
examples.en: The device is faulty. Therefore I would like to send it back.

examples.de: Robbi ist laut. Deswegen schläft Mira schlecht.
examples.en: Robbi is loud. That's why Mira sleeps badly.

deeper.text: daher has a second, older meaning: 'from there'. Daher kommt das Problem means 'That is where the problem comes from'. So when you hear daher with kommen, it often points to a source, not a result. In a sentence like Der Akku ist schwach. Daher kommt das Problem. both ideas meet: the weak battery is the source, and the problem is what follows.

example.de: Der Akku ist schwach. Daher kommt das Problem.
example.en: The battery is weak. That's where the problem comes from.

cards.more: Think of clothes. deshalb, deswegen and darum are your jeans: good for every day, with friends, in the WG kitchen. daher is your shirt for a meeting: still normal, but it looks a little more serious, so it fits a complaint e-mail to TechnoMax. You don't need different grammar for different clothes. All four sit in the same place and pull the verb right behind them. Pick one, and if you used it already, take another to sound less repetitive.

cards.title: Where the word sits: position 1 or after the verb
cards.body: Two places. Position 1: Deshalb → verb → subject (Deshalb schickt Ben Robbi zurück.). Or after the verb and subject, in the middle: Ben schickt Robbi deshalb zurück. With a modal or the Perfekt the second verb part still goes to the very end: Darum hat Ben beim Kundenservice angerufen.
cards.lead: You have four words for a result. Now we look at where they can stand: at the start of the sentence or in the middle, and what happens to the verbs.

examples.de: Ben schickt Robbi deshalb zurück.
examples.en: So Ben sends Robbi back.
examples.why: In the middle: the subject keeps position 1.

examples.de: Darum hat Ben beim Kundenservice angerufen.
examples.en: That's why Ben called customer service.
examples.why: Perfekt: the participle goes to the end.

examples.de: Mira kann deswegen nicht schlafen.
examples.en: That's why Mira can't sleep.
examples.why: Modal: the infinitive goes to the end.

deeper.text: In the middle, the word likes to stand after short pronouns but before nicht. You say Ben schickt ihn deshalb zurück, not Ben schickt deshalb ihn zurück. Little words like ihn, es, sich slip in first, and deshalb follows. The same with a reflexive verb: Mira ärgert sich deshalb. Big new information, like a long object, can still come after deshalb.

example.de: Mira ärgert sich deshalb sehr.
example.en: That's why Mira is very annoyed.

cards.more: Think of a sentence as a row of chairs. The verb always sits on chair 2; it never gives up that chair. Chair 1 can be taken by the subject (Ben) or by deshalb. If deshalb takes chair 1, Ben has to move to chair 3, behind the verb. If Ben keeps chair 1, deshalb simply sits further back in the middle. The last chair stays reserved for the second verb part: zurück, angerufen, schlafen. Nobody steals that chair either.

cards.title: darum: result word or da-word?
cards.body: darum has two jobs. As a result word it means 'that's why' and stands alone: Der Akku ist leer. Darum funktioniert Robbi nicht. As a da-word it replaces um + a thing after a verb with um: Ich kümmere mich um das Problem → Ich kümmere mich darum. Tip: if the verb needs um, darum is a da-word.
cards.lead: darum appeared on the last cards as a result word. But you met it before in A2 chapter 11 as a da-word. This card helps you tell the two apart quickly.

examples.de: Der Akku ist leer. Darum funktioniert Robbi nicht.
examples.en: The battery is empty. That's why Robbi doesn't work.
examples.why: Result word: 'that's why'.

examples.de: Ich kümmere mich darum.
examples.en: I'll take care of it.
examples.why: Da-word: sich kümmern um + it.

examples.de: Die Mitarbeiterin kümmert sich sofort darum.
examples.en: The employee takes care of it right away.
examples.why: Da-word: the verb kümmern needs um.

deeper.text: In everyday talk, Darum! alone is a cheeky answer to Warum?. It means 'just because' and gives no real reason, a bit like a parent who does not want to explain. Warum machst du das? – Darum! It is fine with friends, but never use it with the Kundenservice or in a complaint: there you give a real reason with weil or deshalb.

example.de: Warum machst du das? – Darum!
example.en: Why are you doing that? – Just because!

cards.more: Imagine darum as a person with two jobs. In the morning it works as a signpost: 'that's why, look at what comes next'. Then it stands at the start or in the middle and the verb follows. In the afternoon it works as a stand-in: it takes the place of 'um + a thing' after verbs like sich kümmern um or bitten um. To know which job it has, look at the verb. Does the verb need um? Then darum is the stand-in, the da-word.

rows: means 'that's why'; the verb comes right after it
the verb needs um (sich kümmern um)

cards.title: A morning in the WG: Robbi kept everyone awake
cards.body: Mira and Ben talk in the kitchen. Listen for the result words: each problem leads to a result. Note the chunk Das kann doch nicht wahr sein! (That can't be true!): learn it as one piece for when you are surprised and annoyed.
cards.lead: Time to see all four result words working together in a real conversation, plus one useful chunk for moments when something goes really wrong.

examples.de: Robbi war laut. Deshalb habe ich schlecht geschlafen.
examples.en: Robbi was loud. That's why I slept badly.

examples.de: Ich habe ihn deswegen ausgeschaltet.
examples.en: That's why I switched him off.

examples.de: Das kann doch nicht wahr sein!
examples.en: That can't be true!

deeper.text: In Das kann doch nicht wahr sein! the little word doch carries the feeling. Without it, Das kann nicht wahr sein sounds like a calm statement. With doch it sounds surprised and annoyed. Germans have a shorter twin for the same moment: Das gibt's doch nicht! Both are fine with friends and family. With the Kundenservice, stay calm and use them only with a smile.

example.de: Das gibt's doch nicht!
example.en: I don't believe it!

cards.more: Read this like a small play. Mira enters the kitchen with tired eyes. Ben asks why. Mira tells him the cause, and then she tells him the result with deshalb. Ben is shocked and says the chunk. Then he explains what he did about it with deswegen. Notice how natural it sounds when the words take turns: deshalb, deswegen, darum. Germans switch between them so they don't repeat the same word. Try reading the lines aloud with feeling.
steps: Mira: Ich habe schlecht geschlafen.
Ben: Warum? Was war los?
Mira: Robbi war laut. Deshalb habe ich schlecht geschlafen.
Ben: Das kann doch nicht wahr sein! Er ist doch neu.
Mira: Und der Akku war um zwei Uhr leer. Darum steht er jetzt in der Ecke.
Ben: Ich habe ihn deswegen ausgeschaltet. Heute rufe ich den Kundenservice an.

lessons.title: So laut, dass niemand schlafen kann: sodass and so … dass
lessons.goal: Describe strong consequences in one sentence with sodass and so + adjective + dass, with the verb at the end, also with modal verbs and the Perfekt.

grammar.topic: Consequences with sodass and so … dass
grammar.point: sodass adds the result to the problem in one sentence; a comma comes before it and the conjugated verb goes to the end: Robbi ist laut, sodass niemand schlafen kann. With so + adjective + dass the so stands before the adjective in the first part and makes it stronger: Robbi ist so laut, dass niemand schlafen kann. With a modal or the Perfekt, the conjugated verb is the last word: …, sodass Ben angerufen hat.
grammar.oneLine: Robbi ist so laut, dass niemand schlafen kann.

mistake.wrong: Robbi ist so laut, dass niemand kann schlafen.
mistake.right: Robbi ist so laut, dass niemand schlafen kann.
mistake.why: After dass and sodass the conjugated verb (kann) goes to the very end, behind the infinitive, just like after weil.

terms.meaning: 'so that, with the result that': joins a result to a problem; verb at the end
'so … that': so makes an adjective stronger, dass starts the result
the verb form that changes with the person: kann, hat, stoppt

cards.title: Before we start: from 'deshalb' (verb next) to 'sodass' (verb at the end)
cards.body: Sometimes a problem is so big that you want to say its result in one flowing sentence: Robbi is so loud that nobody can sleep. In lesson 4 you said results with deshalb, darum, deswegen and daher. Today you glue the result to the problem with sodass and with so … dass. Both send the verb to the end.
steps: You already know: deshalb and its friends from lesson 4 (verb right after them) and dass/weil with the verb at the end.
New today: sodass and so + adjective + dass: they give the result and push the verb to the end.
By the end you can: describe Robbi's problems and their strong results in one sentence, also with a modal or the Perfekt.

examples.de: Robbi ist laut. Deshalb kann niemand schlafen.
examples.en: Robbi is loud. That's why nobody can sleep.
examples.why: You know this already: lesson 4.

examples.de: Robbi ist laut, sodass niemand schlafen kann.
examples.en: Robbi is loud, so nobody can sleep.
examples.why: New today: sodass sends kann to the end.

examples.de: Robbi ist so laut, dass niemand schlafen kann.
examples.en: Robbi is so loud that nobody can sleep.
examples.why: New today: so + adjective + dass.

cards.more: Think of two train carriages. Yesterday you parked them next to each other with a full stop between: Robbi ist laut. Deshalb … Today you hook them together with a coupling: sodass or so … dass. Once they are hooked, the second carriage behaves like any dass or weil part you already know: the verb rolls to the very end. Nothing else is new. You will see it with simple verbs first, then with modals and the Perfekt, step by step.

cards.title: sodass: the result, verb at the end
cards.body: sodass (so that, with the result that) adds the result to the problem in the SAME sentence. A comma comes before it. In the sodass part the conjugated verb goes to the END, like after weil or dass: Der Akku ist schwach, sodass Robbi nach zehn Minuten stoppt.
cards.lead: In the intro you saw the coupling between problem and result. This card shows the first coupling, sodass, and where its verb goes.

examples.de: Robbi ist laut, sodass niemand schlafen kann.
examples.en: Robbi is loud, so that nobody can sleep.

examples.de: Der Akku ist schwach, sodass Robbi nach zehn Minuten stoppt.
examples.en: The battery is weak, so Robbi stops after ten minutes.

examples.de: Robbi bleibt unter dem Sofa hängen, sodass Ben ihn suchen muss.
examples.en: Robbi gets stuck under the sofa, so Ben has to look for him.

deeper.text: A weil part can stand at the start: Weil Robbi laut ist, kann niemand schlafen. A sodass part cannot. A result needs its cause first, so the sodass part always comes second, after the comma. If you want the result at the start, use deshalb in a new sentence instead. This keeps the logic in order: first the problem, then what it causes.

example.de: Robbi brummt laut, sodass Frau Webers Katze wegläuft.
example.en: Robbi hums loudly, so Frau Weber's cat runs away.

cards.more: Picture a seesaw. On the left sits the problem: der Akku ist schwach. sodass is the middle bar. On the right sits what happens because of it: Robbi stops. The right side works like every 'little sentence' after weil, dass or wenn: the verb slides down to the very end. A small trick: say the problem, take a breath at the comma, say sodass, and keep the verb in your mouth until the last moment. That pause helps you remember the comma, too.

cards.title: so + adjective + dass: stronger
cards.body: With so … dass the word so goes into the FIRST part, right before an adjective: so laut, so schwer, so kompliziert. It makes the adjective stronger ('so loud that …'). Then a comma, dass, and the result with the verb at the end: Die Anleitung ist so kompliziert, dass niemand sie versteht.
cards.lead: sodass glued two parts together as one word. Now we split it: so moves into the first part and makes an adjective stronger, and dass starts the result.

examples.de: Das Paket war so schwer, dass Ben es nicht tragen konnte.
examples.en: The parcel was so heavy that Ben couldn't carry it.

examples.de: Der Akku ist so schwach, dass Robbi nach zehn Minuten stoppt.
examples.en: The battery is so weak that Robbi stops after ten minutes.

examples.de: Die Anleitung ist so kompliziert, dass niemand sie versteht.
examples.en: The instructions are so complicated that nobody understands them.

deeper.text: You may also see so dass written as two words for the plain result: Robbi ist laut, so dass niemand schlafen kann. Both spellings are correct and mean exactly the same; the one-word sodass is more common today. Don't mix this up with so + adjective + dass: there, so belongs to the adjective and stays in the first part, far away from dass.

example.de: Robbi ist laut, so dass niemand schlafen kann.
example.en: Robbi is loud, so nobody can sleep.

cards.more: Think of a volume knob. laut is loud. so laut turns the knob up: really, really loud. And then dass tells you what this loud volume does to the world: nobody can sleep. In English it is the same: 'so loud that …'. The good news is that German and English put the words in almost the same places. The only German twist is in the dass part: the verb waits until the end, as always after dass.

cards.title: sodass or so … dass?
cards.body: sodass gives a general result: Robbi ist laut, sodass niemand schläft. so … dass stresses HOW strong something is: Robbi ist so laut, dass niemand schläft. Ask yourself: is there an adjective I want to make stronger? Yes → so + adjective + dass. No adjective, or no stress → sodass. Both send the verb to the end.
cards.lead: You now know both couplings. This card gives you one simple question that helps you pick the right one in a second.

examples.de: Robbi stößt gegen die Wände, sodass Ben wütend ist.
examples.en: Robbi bumps into the walls, so Ben is angry.
examples.why: No adjective to stress: sodass.

examples.de: Ben ist so wütend, dass er sofort anruft.
examples.en: Ben is so angry that he calls right away.
examples.why: Stress on wütend: so … dass.

examples.de: Das Geräusch nervt, sodass Mira Musik hört.
examples.en: The noise is annoying, so Mira listens to music.

deeper.text: so … dass works with more than adjectives. With so viel or so oft you can stress an amount or how often something happens: Robbi stößt so oft gegen die Wand, dass Ben ihn ausschaltet. In the same way: Ben arbeitet so viel, dass er keine Zeit zum Putzen hat. The pattern stays the same: so + the word you stress, then dass and the verb at the end.

example.de: Robbi stößt so oft gegen die Wand, dass Ben ihn ausschaltet.
example.en: Robbi bumps into the wall so often that Ben switches him off.

cards.more: Imagine two kinds of arrows. sodass is a normal arrow: this happened, and so that happened. so … dass is an arrow with an exclamation mark: this was SO strong that something happened. When you tell a friend about a really bad day, you want the exclamation mark: Der Bus war so voll, dass ich stehen musste! When you write a calm report, sodass is often enough. Pick the arrow that fits your feeling, then send the verb to the end.

rows: Is there an adjective I want to stress?
at the end of the result part

cards.title: Three ways, one story
cards.body: One problem, three ways to tell it. weil gives the cause, verb at the end. deshalb gives the result, verb right after it. sodass gives the result, verb at the end. Look at the word ORDER after the comma: deshalb kann niemand … but sodass niemand … kann. That is the only difference between the last two.
cards.lead: You have collected weil, deshalb and sodass. This card puts all three next to each other, so you can switch between them without mixing up the word order.

examples.de: Niemand kann schlafen, weil Robbi laut ist.
examples.en: Nobody can sleep because Robbi is loud.
examples.why: weil: cause, verb at the end.

examples.de: Robbi ist laut, deshalb kann niemand schlafen.
examples.en: Robbi is loud, that's why nobody can sleep.
examples.why: deshalb: result, verb next.

examples.de: Robbi ist laut, sodass niemand schlafen kann.
examples.en: Robbi is loud, so nobody can sleep.
examples.why: sodass: result, verb at the end.

deeper.text: In relaxed talk Germans often use also for a result: Der Akku ist leer, also lädt Ben ihn auf. also means 'so' here, not 'also'. It works like deshalb: the verb comes right after it. Watch out for this false friend: English 'also' is German auch. So also and deshalb take the verb next; only sodass sends it to the end.

example.de: Der Akku ist leer, also lädt Ben ihn auf.
example.en: The battery is empty, so Ben charges it.

cards.more: Imagine three doors to the same room. Behind every door is the same fact: Robbi is loud and nobody sleeps. The weil door opens from the back: you enter at the cause. The deshalb door and the sodass door both open at the result, but they have different handles. Behind deshalb the verb jumps up at once. Behind sodass the verb walks slowly to the end of the room. Practise opening all three doors with the same sentence until it feels easy.
steps: weil (cause, verb at the end): Ben ruft an, weil Robbi defekt ist.
deshalb (result, verb next): Robbi ist defekt, deshalb ruft Ben an.
sodass (result, verb at the end): Robbi ist defekt, sodass Ben anruft.

cards.title: With a modal or the Perfekt: two verbs at the end
cards.body: If the result has a modal verb or the Perfekt, both verb parts go to the end. The infinitive or participle comes first, the conjugated verb is the very last word: …, sodass Mira nicht schlafen konnte. / …, sodass Ben beim Kundenservice angerufen hat.
cards.lead: So far the result part had one verb. Real life needs more: 'could not sleep', 'has called'. This card shows how two verbs line up at the end.

examples.de: Robbi war sehr laut, sodass Mira nicht schlafen konnte.
examples.en: Robbi was very loud, so Mira couldn't sleep.

examples.de: Robbi ist kaputtgegangen, sodass Ben beim Kundenservice angerufen hat.
examples.en: Robbi broke, so Ben called customer service.

examples.de: Der Schaden ist so groß, dass Ben das Gerät reparieren lassen will.
examples.en: The damage is so big that Ben wants to have the device repaired.

deeper.text: Separable verbs join up again at the end of a sodass part. In a main clause anrufen splits: Ben ruft sofort an. After sodass the two pieces stick together as one word: …, sodass Ben sofort anruft. The same happens with ausschalten and zurückschicken: …, sodass Mira Robbi ausschaltet. So if you see a long verb at the end, check if it is a split verb that has come home.

example.de: Robbi ist laut, sodass Mira ihn ausschaltet.
example.en: Robbi is loud, so Mira switches him off.

cards.more: Think of a queue at the bus stop. The conjugated verb (konnte, hat, will) is the polite one: in a sodass part it always lets the others go first and stands at the very end of the queue. Just before it stands its partner, the infinitive or participle: schlafen konnte, angerufen hat. With lassen there can even be three: reparieren lassen will. Read them from the back: will, then lassen, then reparieren. The last word is always the one that changes with the person.

cards.title: Ben's notes before the call
cards.body: Before Ben phones TechnoMax, he writes short notes. Then he turns each note into a full sentence with sodass or so … dass. This is a great way to prepare any complaint: first the facts in two or three words, then the full sentence with the result.
cards.lead: Now you can build results with one or two verbs at the end. Here you use that skill the way Ben does: from short notes to clear sentences.

examples.de: Robbi ist so laut, dass niemand schlafen kann.
examples.en: Robbi is so loud that nobody can sleep.

examples.de: Der Akku ist schwach, sodass Robbi nur die Küche putzt.
examples.en: The battery is weak, so Robbi only cleans the kitchen.

examples.de: Robbi bleibt oft am Teppich hängen, sodass Ben ihn tragen muss.
examples.en: Robbi often gets stuck on the carpet, so Ben has to carry him.

deeper.text: nerven is a very common everyday verb: Das nervt! means 'That's annoying!'. You can also say who is annoyed: Robbi nervt mich. Germans use it with friends, at home, at work. In a formal complaint it is too casual; there you write ärgerlich instead: Das ist sehr ärgerlich. So you need both words: nerven for the WG kitchen, ärgerlich for the e-mail.

example.de: Das Geräusch nervt mich total.
example.en: The noise really annoys me.

cards.more: Think of a shopping list. You never write 'I would like to buy one litre of milk, please' on it. You just write 'Milch'. Ben's notes work the same way: laut → niemand schläft. In the shop, or on the phone, you turn the list back into full sentences. The arrow in the note is exactly where sodass or so … dass will go. That is a small trick for every complaint: note the problem, draw an arrow, then fill the arrow with sodass.
steps: laut → niemand schläft: Robbi ist so laut, dass niemand schlafen kann.
Akku schwach → putzt nur die Küche: Der Akku ist schwach, sodass Robbi nur die Küche putzt.
bleibt am Teppich hängen → Ben muss ihn tragen: …, sodass Ben ihn tragen muss.
Motor brummt → Mira hört Musik: Der Motor brummt, sodass Mira mit Kopfhörern Musik hört.

check.hint: Where does the conjugated verb go after dass?

check.hint: After sodass the separable verb joins up again at the very end.

check.explanation: Stress on an adjective → so + adjective + dass.

check.hint: Three verbs at the end; the one that changes with Ben is last.
check.explanation: …, dass Ben das Gerät reparieren lassen will.

check.explanation: The sodass part always comes second.
